svg.font-family: Inter, Segoe UI, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif
svg.title: Figure 2. What renting a server moves, and what it does not remove
svg.desc: A trust ledger in three panels. Before, with no tunnel, your internet provider sees every destination, your address is assigned by them and often shared behind carrier grade translation, and they are a regulated company in your own country with a published legal process. After, with your own rented server, your provider sees only encrypted packets to one address, but the hosting company now sees every destination at the exit and holds administrative access to the machine underneath yours, including memory and disk snapshots that guest disk encryption does not prevent while the machine runs. The exit address is used by exactly one person and is rented in your name with your payment card. The third panel states what moved: control rises, anonymity falls, and the third party is replaced rather than removed. A band below states the four things self-hosting genuinely buys, phrased precisely.
svg.text: Figure 2: What Renting a Server Moves, and What It Does Not Remove
The usual claim is that you trust yourself instead of a company. You do not. You trust a different company, about a machine you do not physically hold.
the situation you are trying to improve

g.text: Who sees your destinations
Your internet provider, all of them,
every day.
What your address says
Assigned by that provider, frequently
shared with other subscribers behind
carrier translation, and it changes.
Who that party is
A regulated company in your own
country, with a published process for
handling legal requests.
Bad for confidentiality. Not bad for
blending in: you look like a household
among many identical households.
Who sees your destinations
Your provider sees only encrypted
packets to one address. Good.
The hosting company sees every
destination, at the exit, in clear.
And more than that
They hold administrative access to the
machine underneath yours: memory and
disk snapshots. Encrypting the guest
disk does not remove them, because the
key sits in memory while it runs.
What your address says
Used by exactly one person. Rented in
your name, with your card, at a company
that keeps that record.

svg.text: three entries, and only one goes up

g.text: Control: up, genuinely
You choose the resolver, the routing,
the software version, and you can read
the configuration yourself instead of
reading a marketing page about it.
Anonymity: down, measurably
A commercial exit puts you in a pool of
strangers on one address. Your own
server is a set of one, and it is the
same one every single day.
Third party: replaced, not removed
You did not take a company out of the
path. You swapped a company that sells
privacy for one that sells servers and
promises nothing about your traffic.

svg.text: What self-hosting does buy, stated precisely, because it is worth having

g.text: An exit whose configuration you can read. No no-logs claim to evaluate, because you can look. Lesson 6.3 spent its length on the fact that you cannot do this with a provider.
A fixed address you control. Allow lists, remote access, and services that object to shared exits. This is the use case with no commercial substitute.
Protection from the local network, which is a real threat and a small one. Against a hostile hotel or coffee shop this works exactly as advertised.
The knowledge. After building this you can read any provider's configuration and say what it does. That transfers to every other network you touch.
Note what is not on that list: anonymity, and hiding from anybody with a legal process. If those are the goal, this build makes them worse, not better.

svg.text: Lesson 6.1 set out that a VPN moves who can see your traffic rather than removing the observer. Renting your own server is the same move, one step further along.
Build it for control, for a fixed address, or to learn. Those are good reasons. Do not build it to disappear.
And be honest about the last row: you are also now the person legally answerable for every packet that leaves that address.
